title: Module Header: Structural Properties of Euler's Totient
content: The file imports Mathlib's Nat.Totient, ZMod.Basic, and Tactic modules. The module docstring (lines 5-33) describes six classes of structural results: parity, prime characterization, divisibility, super-multiplicativity, the product formula, and the GCD-totient identity. The namespace `EulerTotientOQ03` opens `Nat` and `Finset` for convenient access to totient lemmas and finite set operations.
mathContext: Euler's totient $\varphi(n)$ counts the integers in $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ coprime to $n$. These structural properties reveal how $\varphi$ interacts with divisibility, prime factorization, and the group structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$.

title: Parity: phi(n) Is Even for n >= 3
content:
`totient_even` (lines 44-45) proves that phi(n) is even when n > 2. The proof in Mathlib uses the involution a -> -a on (Z/nZ)*: for n > 2, this involution has no fixed points (since a = -a implies n | 2a, impossible for coprime a when n > 2), so elements pair up and the group has even order.

`totient_odd_iff` (lines 48-49) and `totient_eq_one_iff` (lines 52-53) establish the complementary characterizations: phi(n) is odd iff n in {1,2}, and phi(n) = 1 iff n in {1,2}.
mathContext: The involution $a \mapsto -a = n-a$ on $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$ is fixed-point-free for $n > 2$: if $a \equiv -a \pmod{n}$, then $n \mid 2a$. Since $\gcd(a,n) = 1$, we need $n \mid 2$, so $n \leq 2$. This pairs all $\varphi(n)$ elements into distinct pairs, giving $2 \mid \varphi(n)$.

title: Prime Characterization: phi(n) = n-1 iff n Is Prime
content:
`totient_eq_sub_one_iff_prime` (lines 63-65) proves that phi(p) = p-1 if and only if p is prime (for p > 0). The 'only if' direction is the content: if every element of {1,...,n-1} is coprime to n, then n has no proper divisors between 1 and n, so n is prime.

The supporting lemmas establish bounds: `totient_lt` (phi(n) < n for n > 1, since 0 is never coprime to n > 0), `totient_le` (phi(n) <= n always), and `totient_pos` (phi(n) > 0 iff n > 0).
mathContext: $\varphi(n) = n-1$ means every element of $\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$ is coprime to $n$, i.e., $n$ has no divisor $d$ with $1 < d < n$. This is exactly the definition of primality. The characterization makes $\varphi$ a 'primality detector': $n$ is prime iff $\varphi(n)$ achieves its maximum value $n-1$.

title: Divisibility: a | b Implies phi(a) | phi(b), and Super-Multiplicativity
content:
`totient_dvd_of_dvd` (lines 89-91) proves that if a divides b then phi(a) divides phi(b). This follows from the surjective ring homomorphism Z/bZ -> Z/aZ (reduction mod a), which restricts to a surjection on unit groups.

`totient_super_multiplicative` (lines 97-99) proves phi(a)*phi(b) <= phi(ab). Equality holds iff gcd(a,b) = 1 (the multiplicativity from OQ-02). The gap is quantified by the GCD-totient identity in Part V.

The prime-specific formulas (lines 101-109) compute phi(pn) = p*phi(n) when p | n and phi(pn) = (p-1)*phi(n) when p does not divide n.
mathContext: The surjection $(\mathbb{Z}/b\mathbb{Z})^* \twoheadrightarrow (\mathbb{Z}/a\mathbb{Z})^*$ (for $a \mid b$) gives $\varphi(a) \mid \varphi(b)$ by the first isomorphism theorem. Super-multiplicativity $\varphi(a)\varphi(b) \leq \varphi(ab)$ follows from CRT: the natural map $(\mathbb{Z}/ab\mathbb{Z})^* \to (\mathbb{Z}/a\mathbb{Z})^* \times (\mathbb{Z}/b\mathbb{Z})^*$ is injective (CRT), giving $\varphi(ab) \geq \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$.

title: Euler's Product Formula: phi(n) = n * prod(1 - 1/p)
content:
Three equivalent forms of Euler's product formula:

1. `totient_product_formula` (lines 122-124): The rational form phi(n) = n * prod_{p|n}(1 - 1/p), stated over Q.

2. `totient_factorization_formula` (lines 127-129): Natural number form using the prime factorization: phi(n) = prod_{(p,k) in factorization(n)} p^(k-1)*(p-1).

3. `totient_div_form` (lines 133-136): Division form: phi(n) = (n / prod primes) * prod(p-1).

All three encode the same information but in different algebraic contexts (Q, N with factorization, N with division).
mathContext: The product formula $\varphi(n) = n \prod_{p \mid n}(1 - 1/p)$ follows from multiplicativity: $\varphi(n) = \prod_{p^k \| n} \varphi(p^k) = \prod_{p^k \| n} p^{k-1}(p-1) = n \prod_{p \mid n} (1 - 1/p)$. This is an inclusion-exclusion over prime divisors: start with $n$ integers, remove multiples of each prime $p$ (fraction $1/p$), add back doubly-removed ones, etc.

title: The GCD-Totient Identity
content:
`totient_gcd_mul` (lines 156-159) proves the identity phi(gcd(a,b)) * phi(ab) = phi(a) * phi(b) * gcd(a,b). This single identity unifies:
- Multiplicativity: when gcd(a,b) = 1, phi(1)*phi(ab) = phi(a)*phi(b)*1, so phi(ab) = phi(a)*phi(b).
- Divisibility + product: when a | b, gcd(a,b) = a, so phi(a)*phi(ab) = phi(a)*phi(b)*a, giving phi(ab) = phi(b)*a.

The identity is a manifestation of the 'CRT with overlap' principle: the natural map (Z/abZ)* -> (Z/aZ)* x (Z/bZ)* has kernel of size gcd(a,b)/phi(gcd(a,b)).
mathContext: The identity $\varphi(\gcd(a,b)) \cdot \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a) \cdot \varphi(b) \cdot \gcd(a,b)$ is proved by reducing to prime powers via multiplicativity and checking the identity for $a = p^i$, $b = p^j$. For a single prime power: $\varphi(p^{\min(i,j)}) \cdot \varphi(p^{i+j}) = \varphi(p^i) \cdot \varphi(p^j) \cdot p^{\min(i,j)}$, which reduces to a straightforward calculation with $p^k(p-1)$ terms.

title: Concrete Verifications
content:
Concrete examples verifying each structural property:
- Parity: phi(3) = 2, phi(4) = 2, phi(12) = 4 are all even.
- Odd totient: phi(1) = phi(2) = 1.
- Prime characterization: phi(7) = 6 = 7-1; phi(9) = 6 != 8 = 9-1.
- Super-multiplicativity with strict inequality: phi(2)*phi(4) = 2 < 4 = phi(8).
- Divisibility: 4 | 12, so phi(4) = 2 divides phi(12) = 4.
- GCD identity: phi(gcd(6,10))*phi(60) = phi(6)*phi(10)*gcd(6,10) = 16.
- Product formula: phi(30) = 8.

All verified by `native_decide` or explicit witnesses.
mathContext: These examples illustrate edge cases and non-trivial instances. The strict super-multiplicativity phi(2)*phi(4) = 2 < 4 = phi(8) shows that non-coprime factors inflate the product. The GCD identity check with 6 and 10 (gcd = 2) demonstrates the formula in a non-trivial case.
